title: The Fastest Way to Lose Credibility With a New Leader
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership Field Note argues that team members who meet a new leader by promoting their own accomplishments damage the very credibility they want to build. Seasoned leaders know that nearly everyone is auditioning in the first 100 days and so they discount self-promotion. A stronger approach is to show situational awareness and to deliver uncomfortable news about risks and opportunities. The piece says even that falls short of what earns real trust. The most credible move is to say what the organisation needs, even when the assessment is inconvenient for the speaker personally. Advice that is visibly unfiltered by self-interest is the clearest signal of trustworthy judgment, and the writer concludes that the people who earn trust in a transition are the ones trying to be useful rather than to look good.
points: Leading with a resume in a leadership transition reads as auditioning, so new leaders discount it and the effort backfires.
Naming the risks, opportunities and avoided truths shows situational awareness, which the piece ranks as wiser but still not enough.
The strongest credibility signal is an assessment of what the function needs that holds whether or not the speaker is chosen for the role.
Separating a recommendation from one's own fate shows that the organisation comes before the person, which new leaders notice immediately.
The transition window is when a leader forms lasting judgments, so the goal should be usefulness rather than image.
quotes: When a new leader arrives, most team members instinctively shift into impression-management mode. They highlight their significant accomplishments, position their skills, and look for opportunities to demonstrate their value.
Seasoned leaders have seen this before. They know that nearly everyone they meet in the first 100 days is auditioning. And because they know it, they discount it.
The team member who leads with their resume sparks skepticism, not confidence. The very behavior intended to build credibility erodes it.

The most credible thing a team member can do in the early days of a leadership transition is to identify what the organization really needs — even when that assessment is inconvenient for them personally.
They have put the organization before themselves. They have separated their recommendation from their fate. That is instantly and unmistakably credible.
Most people spend that window trying to look good. The ones who earn real trust spend it trying to be useful.
